name: Priya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Meadowfield Dairy, the Hartley family's farm. It's 350 cows, two milking robots already, plus grass silage and maize for feed. My day starts at six with the robot reports on my phone, which cows didn't come in to be milked, which ones have a high cell count, that's an early sign of an udder infection. Then I go and find those cows, check feet, help with calving, and clean down. I've been there a year and a bit, and the cows still know more than I do.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a corner shop with my husband Farid for twenty-five years. Six in the morning till ten at night, newspapers, milk, lottery tickets. We sold it two years ago, and I didn't want to sit still, so I answered the Hartleys' advert. I use the AI on my phone all day, to read the robot data, to look up cow diseases, even to help write the vet's notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, at least the robots we've got keep working. I'd say it to the Hartleys and to the family on our group chat. I'd still tell people to learn the tools, because they make life easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I carry on getting better at the job, and that's fine. I like the farm and the cows. I was quite looking forward to seeing what else these tools could do, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Meadowfield and keep using the AI to learn faster. Money-wise nothing changes. We have the three rental flats from our shop years and they pay steadily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like most about the work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cows, honestly. In the shop, the customers grumbled. A cow just wants feeding, milking and a clean bed, and if you give her that she gives you forty litres a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always: work hard, look after your family, and don't wait for anyone to give you anything. My father had a market stall, then a shop, and I had a shop. You build things yourself.

S0.say: I'd say at least the robots we've got keep working, to the owners and the family chat. I'd still tell people to learn the tools because they make life easier.
S0.think: I carry on getting better at the job, and that's fine because I like the farm and the cows. I was looking forward to seeing what else the tools could do.
S0.do: Keeps working at the dairy and using AI to learn faster. Leaves money plans as they are, with three rental flats from her shop years paying steadily.
S0.quote: A cow just wants feeding, milking and a clean bed, and if you give her that she gives you forty litres a day.
S0.fieldNote: Priya runs her farm job like a shopkeeper: early start, data first, hard work. She already works with milking robots and uses AI all day. Self-reliance from her family's market stall and shop shapes her outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and learn. It's what we did with the shop when card machines and self-checkouts came in. The ones who adapted survived, the ones who complained closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be useful. I already read the robot reports better than the Hartleys' son, and he's thirty. If they get more robots, they need someone who understands them and the cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Hartleys for more responsibility with the robots and offer to do the manufacturer's training. I'd look at buying a share in a small farm, maybe with my nephew who wants to farm, with robots from day one. We've got money from the flats and the shop sale, so that's not a fantasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do people say when you tell them this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm 58 and I'll be stopping soon. But I'm not stopping, I'm changing. Women in my family work until they can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you do it with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nephew Amir, he's 27, agricultural college. He's got the knowledge, I've got the money and the business sense. We'd buy forty hectares with a robot milker and run it properly.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and learn, like when card machines and self-checkouts came into shops. The ones who adapted survived; the ones who complained closed.
S1.think: I think I'd be useful, because I already read the robot reports better than the owners' 30-year-old son. More robots means they need someone who understands them and the cows.
S1.do: Asks the owners for more responsibility with the robots and takes the manufacturer's training. Looks at buying a share in a small farm with robots from day one, using money from the flats and shop sale, with her nephew.
S1.feel: Calm and even a bit excited.
S1.quote: I'm not stopping, I'm changing. Women in my family work until they can't.
S1.fieldNote: She sees disruption as a market opportunity, using her shop experience as proof. Her money lets her plan to buy a farm share, not just survive. Family is both her workforce and her safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, even for me. Businesses need time to adapt, and governments shouldn't panic and start throwing money around. But I'd want them to make sure the big tech firms play by the same rules as everybody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job goes by 60, and I'd be fine. What worries me is our tenants. If they all lose their jobs at once, who pays the rent on the flats? Our steady income becomes not steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, I'd sell one of the three flats while prices are good and put the money somewhere safer, and maybe some into the robot companies. I'd drop the farm-share plan with Amir, it's too risky with two years. Once it hit, I'd help my children however they needed, and I'd keep the other two flats and be patient with tenants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More for the money than the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years of warning. What does that short window take away from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time to build something. With five or ten years, Amir and I could buy the farm and get it running. With two years, everything would be up in the air, prices, buyers, banks. You don't open a shop in a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faisal, my middle son, works in IT support. He'd be first out. I'd tell him to come home if he needs to, and we'd sort it out as a family, the way we always have.

S2.say: I'd say this is too fast, even for me. Businesses need time and governments shouldn't panic, but the big tech firms should play by the same rules as everybody else.
S2.think: My job goes by 60 and I'd be fine. What worries me is tenants losing their jobs at once and not paying rent on our flats.
S2.do: Sells one of three rental flats while prices are good and puts the money somewhere safer, partly into robot companies. Drops the farm-share plan with her nephew and helps her children as needed, especially her son in IT support.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more about money than about the job.
S2.quote: You don't open a shop in a storm.
S2.fieldNote: Her unease is a landlord's and investor's, not a worker's. She cancels her own expansion because two years is too short to build. Family, not the state, is her plan for her son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for those who are willing. I'd say get learning, get saving and help your family. I'd also say the government should keep things simple and fair and not get in people's way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's good. I'd be 63, I'd have five years to build something with Amir, and then the robots would do the heavy work. I'd be the owner, not the worker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd do the robot training at Meadowfield and start looking at land with Amir. Next year we'd buy, with robot milkers from the start. I'd keep the flats but put away a bit extra in case tenants struggle later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, pleased, a little nervous, like opening the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Couldn't the farm fail, if AGI arrives in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course I could. We nearly lost the shop in the first year, when the supermarket opened on the bypass. We survived because we were open longer and knew every customer's name. With the farm, I'd make sure it's small and debt-free, so if it fails we don't lose the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Farid say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farid would say 'again?' and roll his eyes. Then he'd do the accounts, like always.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for those who are willing: get learning, get saving and help your family. Government should keep things simple and fair and not get in people's way.
S3.think: For me it's good: at 63 I'd have five years to build something with my nephew, and robots would do the heavy work. I'd be the owner, not the worker.
S3.do: Does robot training at the dairy this year and starts looking at land with her nephew, buying next year with robot milkers from the start. Keeps the flats but saves extra in case tenants struggle, and keeps the farm small and debt-free.
S3.feel: Calm, busy and pleased, a little nervous, like opening the shop.
S3.quote: Farid would say 'again?' and roll his eyes. Then he'd do the accounts, like always.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is long enough for her to switch from worker to owner, which she clearly wants. Her caution, debt-free and small, comes from nearly losing the shop. Her marriage is a working partnership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for anyone with sense. I'd tell young people to learn a skill and own something. I'd say owning is the safest thing when machines do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd be 68, I'd have had time to run a small farm with Amir and hand it over to him. That's a good ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training, buy into the farm with Amir in a year or two, and run it till I'm 65 or so. I'd keep the flats and save a bit more each year. And I'd tell my grandchildren to own something, even something small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep coming back to owning things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owning is what saved my family. My father came with nothing and had a market stall. If you own the robot, the robot works for you. If you don't, you work for the man who does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people would say that's easy for someone with savings. What would you say to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. Not everyone has money. That's why family matters, and community. People should help each other first. I don't trust big programmes.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone with sense, and young people should learn a skill and own something. Owning is the safest thing when machines do the work.
S4.think: It's comfortable for me: at 68 I'd have had time to run a small farm with my nephew and hand it over. That's a good ending.
S4.do: Does the robot training, buys into a farm with her nephew within a year or two and runs it till about 65. Keeps the flats, saves a bit more each year and tells her grandchildren to own something.
S4.quote: If you own the robot, the robot works for you. If you don't, you work for the man who does.
S4.fieldNote: Her core belief is ownership, rooted in her father's market stall. She admits that not everyone has money and turns to family and community rather than big programmes. The long window gives her the ending she wants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because nobody could build anything in that time and our tenants would struggle. What would help is stable rules, fair taxes and banks still lending to small businesses, so families can buy machines and own their own work. And not big handouts that make people wait instead of doing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why a shopkeeper went to cows. It's simple. After twenty-five years counting other people's change, I wanted to be tired from real work, with mud on my boots.

headlineQuote: After twenty-five years counting other people's change, I wanted to be tired from real work, with mud on my boots.
portrait: Priya Rahman is 58 and ran a corner shop with her husband for twenty-five years before selling it and joining Meadowfield Dairy, a farm that already uses milking robots. She starts each day with the robot reports on her phone and uses AI constantly to learn faster. With three rental flats and the shop money, she sees change mainly as a chance to own something: a small robot dairy run with her nephew. Only the two-year AGI picture makes her uneasy, mostly about tenants unable to pay and her son in IT support, and she would cancel her farm plan rather than build in a storm. She believes in ownership, family and self-reliance over big government programmes.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because nobody could build anything that fast and her tenants would struggle to pay.
whatWouldHelp: Stable rules, fair taxes and banks still lending to small businesses so families can buy machines and own their work, rather than big handouts.
